title: Profile data layout and distinguish memory from locality
summary: Compare complete AoS and SoA records with bounded release profiling, separate phase costs, and measured process memory.
objectives: Explain hot-field locality without claiming a universal cache result.
Preserve complete records while changing layout.
Interpret phase timings, payload capacity, allocation requests and peak RSS separately.
Design a controlled experiment that can disprove a favored explanation.
body:
Purpose: locate a cost before changing the representation

A snapshot service repeatedly totals price times quantity across many records. Its records also contain timestamps, account identifiers, symbols, and audit tags. Those fields remain required, but this query does not read them. The question is precise: does grouping the queried fields into separate contiguous arrays reduce the time for this read-mostly operation while preserving every logical record? This lab investigates that question without changing P12's replay engine or claiming to model an exchange.

The earlier projects taught bounded processing and correct state transitions. Those constraints still apply. A representation change must preserve data, respect memory limits, and produce the same result. Performance is an additional requirement with a named workload, not permission to remove validation or silently discard fields.

Plain model: useful bytes and neighboring bytes

An array of structures, abbreviated AoS, stores complete records consecutively. Here each record occupies 64 bytes on the measured target. A structure of arrays, SoA, stores prices together, quantities together, and cold metadata together. The price and quantity columns together occupy 16 bytes per logical record; all metadata is still retained in another vector. Both layouts hold the same 48,000,000 bytes of reserved element storage for 750,000 records.

Processors transfer memory in blocks and exploit nearby accesses. A scan that needs only two fields may fetch less irrelevant data when those fields are grouped. That is a reason to investigate locality, not a guaranteed speedup. Compiler vectorization, prefetching, cache capacities, alignment, and access order also matter. A query that consumes complete records or frequently inserts and removes rows may favor a different organization.

The example uses repr(C) to make its illustrative field order explicit and prints size_of::<Row>(). Ordinary Rust struct field order is not a wire-format promise. Even a known in-memory layout is not permission to serialize raw padding or reinterpret arbitrary bytes as a valid value. This safe example accesses fields through Rust values throughout.

Predict before measuring

Predict whether SoA must use less total memory, whether it must allocate fewer buffers, and whether its construction phase must be faster. Then identify exactly what the scan timer includes. A useful prediction separates three quantities: retained payload, bytes relevant to a query, and elapsed time. They are related but are not interchangeable.

# Working directory: rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo test -p p12-replay --examples
mise exec -- cargo build --release -p p12-replay --examples
mise exec -- cargo run --release -p p12-replay --example layout_profile -- aos 750000 80
mise exec -- cargo run --release -p p12-replay --example layout_profile -- soa 750000 80

The retained payload is equal because SoA preserves the cold fields. AoS makes one vector reservation; SoA makes three. The measured SoA construction median was higher, even though its repeated scan was faster. Thus neither “more allocations always means slower overall” nor “a faster scan means less resident memory” explains the complete observation.

Runnable example and its boundaries

The command validates a maximum of one million rows and 200 passes before allocation. Count text is bounded, non-Unicode arguments are rejected explicitly, and allocation reservation failures return errors. The fixture generates positive bounded integer prices and quantities. Those closed bounds keep the sum and repeated checksum inside u64; this is not a summation API for arbitrary external numbers.

Construction starts before reserving and filling the vectors. Validation reconstructs every complete record and compares it with the deterministic fixture, including metadata unused by the query. It also obtains an expected numeric result. Two warm-up scans precede the measured scans. The scan timer includes the repeated reductions and their accumulated checksum; it excludes construction, full-record validation, warm-ups, output, and final destruction. black_box discourages optimization based on visible inputs and outputs but is a best-effort tool, not a guarantee about generated instructions.

Guided checkpoint: profile one complete process

On macOS, build once and use the included resource-counter driver. Run from the course root; choose a new output directory for every investigation. The driver refuses an existing directory, alternates variant order across seven pairs, and invokes each sample in a separate process.

python3 projects/reference/p12-replay/profile-layout.py \
  --binary .local/native-target/release/examples/layout_profile \
  --output .local/layout-profile-first

This command assumes the course's mise configuration supplied the build target. If you selected a different target directory, pass the corresponding executable path. The Rust example is portable; this driver specifically uses macOS /usr/bin/time -l. On another operating system, choose its documented profiler and record its units instead of copying macOS counter interpretations.

The outer process timer includes startup, construction, validation, warm-ups, measured scans, output, destruction, and profiler overhead. Maximum resident set size is a process-wide peak. It includes more than vector elements and says nothing about how many allocation requests occurred. The installed macOS getrusage(2) manual identifies this counter's unit as bytes; GNU time commonly reports a different unit. Verify the actual tool rather than trusting a familiar-looking label.

Observed evidence and what it means

The historical recorded release run used Rust 1.99.0 on an Apple M3 Ultra with 28 logical CPUs and 96 GiB of memory. Every sample contained 750,000 records and 80 measured passes, with two warm-ups. All complete-record comparisons passed, and all 14 samples produced checksum 163062480000000. Background load, affinity, power, and thermal state were not controlled.

Measured quantityAoS medianSoA median
Construction4.204 ms5.166 ms
80 scans44.108 ms17.000 ms
Whole observed process58.530 ms31.150 ms
Maximum RSS49,872,896 bytes49,938,432 bytes

The SoA scan median is about 0.385 times the AoS scan median in this experiment. The scan ranges were 42.926–46.589 ms and 15.864–17.429 ms respectively. These are observations of a synthetic hot-field query. They do not establish a universal speedup, a service latency guarantee, or a lower memory requirement. Medians from separate phases should not be added as though they came from one representative execution.

This is resource profiling, not a call-stack or hardware cache-miss profile. Locality is a plausible explanation consistent with the access pattern, while code generation and vectorization are competing explanations. The measurements do not isolate their contributions. Use a suitable CPU profiler or inspect generated code if a decision requires that attribution. Raw process counters and all sample commands are preserved in the linked evidence.

Intentional mistake: time unequal work

In a disposable learner copy, remove the cold metadata vector from SoA and compare it with the original AoS. The full-record validation should prevent this reduced representation from being accepted as equivalent. Treat that failure as expected until you actually run the mutation. A faster program that forgot required data answers a different question. Another misleading comparison would include construction for AoS but time only the reduction for SoA; write both timer boundaries before accepting such a report.

Apply the problem-solving playbook

Observation: the actual SoA scan was faster, but its RSS was slightly higher. Hypothesis A says the improvement occurred because SoA discarded metadata and retained less memory. Hypothesis B says the same data was reorganized so the query accesses a smaller hot subset. Distinguish them by inspecting reserved capacities and comparing every reconstructed field. The actual run retained 48 MB of element storage in both representations and passed full-record comparisons, disproving A for this implementation.

B remains compatible with the evidence, but it is not a complete causal proof: the two loops also give the optimizer different opportunities. A next experiment could add a query that reads every field, holding row count and build profile fixed, or use cache-miss and instruction profiles. State the expected discriminator first. Capture the workload, raw samples, equality evidence, rejected hypothesis, and residual uncertainty in the problem-solving playbook. An AI review should explain those controls before recommending a representation rewrite.

Independent practice, hints, and worked direction

Measure 10,000 rows, then 750,000 rows with the same number of passes. Separately design a whole-record checksum query. Keep all logical fields and compare complete output before timing. Decide whether your application performs enough repeated scans to recover SoA's observed construction cost; do not infer that crossover from this one workload alone.

Hint 1: preserve the experimental cases

Keep samples of different row counts in different directories.

Hint 2: define equivalent work

A whole-record query must read metadata in both variants, not merely return the original notional sum.

Hint 3: choose the request boundary

Report per-sample construction-plus-query totals if that is the real request boundary.

Worked direction

First establish matching results, then repeat each controlled case, and finally choose a representation for the measured workload. A result showing no worthwhile improvement is a useful outcome.

Reconstruct a working checkpoint

From the course root, create a fresh final P12 study copy. The helper preserves originals, copies the exact lockfile, and refuses to overwrite an existing destination. Reuse your prior copy or choose another name when repeating the exercise.

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p12 final --destination learner-work/layout-investigation
mise exec -- cargo test --locked --all-targets --manifest-path learner-work/layout-investigation/Cargo.toml
mise exec -- cargo run --release --locked --manifest-path learner-work/layout-investigation/Cargo.toml --example layout_profile -- aos 750000 80

The P12 checkpoint guide also provides the earlier exact-price milestone. Mise keeps build output in the shared native target.

When you get stuck

Run mise exec -- cargo test -p p12-replay --example layout_profile before examining timing. Confirm --release, the printed row count, and the payload capacity. If memory figures appear absurd, inspect the profiler's units and raw output. If a result differs, reduce to one or 17 records and compare reconstructed fields. Request review with both commands, all samples, equality checks, timer boundaries, and your two competing explanations.

Engineering decisions, evidence limits, and mastery

A bounded immutable fixture and separate phases make this experiment reviewable. Safe vectors and typed records suffice; unsafe pointer traversal or a custom allocator would add obligations without answering the current question. Three buffer reservations are a visible tradeoff for narrower query arrays. Evolve the design only when an actual workload requires different update, ownership, or latency behavior.

The two layout tests passed, strict Clippy passed, and the release example produced 14 successful profiled samples. See commands, source hashes, results and limitations and raw resource counters. Independent review remains pending. Mastery means explaining why equal total memory can coexist with different scan times, identifying an unmeasured causal factor, and proposing the next experiment without claiming the result in advance.

title: Choose ownership and dispatch without hidden cost claims
summary: Trace borrowed and owned parsing, qualify zero-copy claims, and compare static and dynamic dispatch as design choices.
objectives: Distinguish a borrowed symbol slice from an allocation-free program.
Choose retention ownership from required lifetimes.
Explain static and dynamic dispatch separately from heap allocation.
Preserve behavior while deciding which cost would justify measurement.
body:
Purpose: separate ownership, allocation, and dispatch costs

A tick report reads a small bounded text buffer, calculates totals, and sometimes retains records after the buffer is released. Three design questions arise: can symbol text be borrowed, when must it become owned, and how should callers select a calculation? These questions concern different boundaries. A trait object does not inherently allocate, and a borrowed string does not make an entire program allocation-free. This checkpoint keeps those distinctions visible in executable code.

The layout investigation measured a repeated scan. This lesson complements it with ownership and abstraction reasoning. It does not invent a static-versus-dynamic speed result. First establish the behavior and lifetime requirements; then measure only if dispatch or allocation cost is material to the real workload.

Plain model: ownership is a duration requirement

A borrowed &str identifies existing valid UTF-8 bytes without owning their storage. Its lifetime constrains how long a caller may use them. A String owns a growable buffer and can survive the source from which its contents were copied. Our parser borrows symbol slices from one input String, parses prices and quantities into integers, and returns a Vec of typed rows. The vector allocates storage for row descriptors even though the symbol bytes are shared.

“Zero-copy” therefore needs a named boundary: symbol extraction creates slices into the existing buffer. Reading a file or network body may already have copied bytes into that buffer; parsing numeric text computes new integer values; storing the row vector requires memory. Retaining one tiny slice can also keep its entire backing buffer alive. Avoid a broad zero-copy claim when the evidence establishes only one avoided copy.

Predict before running

Predict whether the borrowed rows can outlive the input string, whether &dyn Metric requires a heap allocation, and whether a generic total and a dynamic total should produce identical results. Then run the reference:

# Working directory: rust-course/projects
mise exec -- cargo run -p p12-replay --example dispatch_allocation
mise exec -- cargo test -p p12-replay --example dispatch_allocation

The observed output reports two rows, static notional 7700, and dynamic totals [7700, 5]. After converting the rows into owned records, the program drops both the borrowed vector and source buffer, then reports two retained owned rows. The borrowed rows could not have survived that source drop. The dynamic metrics borrow two values; no Box is required at that interface.

Runnable example: a bounded borrowed parser

The parser checks a 4096-byte input bound and a 64-row limit. Each nonempty record has exactly three comma-separated fields. Symbols contain one through eight uppercase ASCII letters; positive price and quantity have explicit integer limits. Invalid fields produce a typed error. Empty input yields no rows. str::lines() is appropriate here because the complete borrowed input is already bounded; this is different from reading an arbitrarily long file line into memory.

The returned Tick<'_> values carry borrows from the supplied input. The library does not clone the source to appease a compiler error. At the retention boundary, retain explicitly creates owned symbols because the requirement changes: those records must remain usable independently. Both choices are sound first implementations for their respective lifetimes. Borrowing is not automatically superior to ownership.

Follow allocations through the design

The input String owns storage. The parser's row vector can grow as rows are pushed. A vector has a length and capacity; reserving capacity can reduce growth reallocations when a useful bound or accurate estimate is known. Reserving the maximum for every tiny request may waste memory, while requesting exactly one additional slot repeatedly can create needless work. Here at most 64 rows makes ordinary vector growth a proportionate choice.

Each nonempty owned symbol created by to_owned needs independent string storage, and the retained vector owns its own element buffer. These are code-level allocation opportunities, not instrumented allocator-call counts. Compiler transformations, allocator behavior, and capacity policy affect actual requests and operating-system mappings. If allocation is the suspected bottleneck, use an allocation profiler appropriate to the target and measure the chosen request boundary.

Alternatives include processing borrowed rows immediately, retaining the full input together with offsets, sharing a buffer through an ownership type, or copying only records that must survive. Each has a duration and memory tradeoff. A small copy that lets a large network buffer be released may reduce retained memory. Adding reference counting everywhere can introduce metadata, synchronization, and API complexity without serving the current requirement.

Static and dynamic dispatch: the selection boundary

total_static<M: Metric> takes a concrete metric type selected at compile time. The compiler can generate code for the concrete instantiations and may inline their operations. total_dynamic accepts a trait object, enabling a common interface for metric implementations selected at runtime. Its reference carries access to the underlying value and the information needed to call the appropriate methods. The small array can contain both a notional metric and a quantity metric.

Dynamic dispatch does not imply that the metric is boxed: these objects are borrowed. Conversely, a generic function may operate on heap-owned data. Allocation and dispatch are orthogonal decisions. Runtime flexibility can be worth an indirect call; generic specialization can improve optimization opportunities while increasing generated code and compilation work across many instantiations. A compiler may sometimes devirtualize a visible trait-object call, so source syntax alone is not a measured instruction trace.

Neither mechanism is a universally professional or universally fast choice. Use a concrete or generic type when the implementation is naturally fixed. Use a trait object when heterogeneous implementations or runtime selection simplify a real boundary. In a hot path, consider dispatching once around a batch instead of once per element, but preserve the same behavior and measure the change.

Guided checkpoint: retain only when necessary

Trace the input's ownership through main. Calculate the borrowed totals while the input remains alive. Then inspect retain and identify each field copied into the owned representation. Drop the borrowed rows and input and access the owned records. The passing test checks complete expected owned rows, not only their count, so a retention function that accidentally drops a symbol or swaps a quantity is detected.

Now choose a consumer requirement. A report rendered immediately can use the borrowed rows. A background queue that outlives the request needs an appropriate owned representation. Write that lifetime requirement in plain language before selecting String, references, or reference-counted buffers. An API should make the required ownership transition visible instead of hiding an expensive clone inside a convenient accessor.

Intentional mistake: drop the owner too early

In a disposable learner copy, move drop(input) to immediately after parsing, then use the borrowed rows. Predict a borrow-checker rejection because the owner would be moved while references remain in use. This mutation is an expected diagnostic exercise, not an executed check recorded in the supplied logs. Restore the valid lifetime ordering. Changing every field to owned text would satisfy the compiler but would also change the allocation and ownership design; do that only when the retention requirement calls for it.

Apply the problem-solving playbook

Observation: the reference calculates both metrics through &dyn Metric and retains owned records after the source is dropped. Hypothesis A says dynamic dispatch requires boxing and therefore caused the symbol copies. Hypothesis B says the copies occur because the retained records must outlive the input. Inspect the actual boundary: the dynamic metric array borrows values, while to_owned appears specifically in retain. The executed tests verify the totals and retained contents. A's necessary-allocation claim is disproved by this concrete borrowing interface.

For a further distinguishing experiment, remove the retention step in a learner copy while keeping dynamic dispatch. The expected totals stay the same and the explicit symbol-copy step disappears. Conversely, keep retention and use only static totals; ownership still requires those owned strings. Mark these latter experiments as expected until you execute them. Record the result and limitations in the shared investigation template. Ask an AI assistant to identify the owning allocation and relevant lifetime before accepting a proposed clone or lifetime annotation.

Independent tasks, tiered hints, and worked solution

Investigate adding a maximum-price metric: decide whether the summation interface can express it correctly, and design a corresponding aggregation if it cannot. Then change the application to retain only rows whose quantity exceeds two. Specify whether order is preserved and whether the original input may be released afterward. Add a test containing zero retained rows and another containing two symbols with different quantities.

Hint 1: check the aggregation contract

A metric's return value must fit the existing result contract; a sum interface does not compute a maximum. A maximum operation needs a corresponding aggregation function, returning Option for empty input.

Hint 2: follow the owner

Filtering borrowed rows does not extend their lifetime.

Hint 3: place the ownership transition

Perform the filter before copying symbols if the goal is selective retention.

Worked solution direction

The worked direction is to add a separate maximum-price function using Iterator::max, with static or dynamic field selection only if that abstraction helps. For selective retention, iterate in source order, filter by quantity, and construct owned rows only for matches. An empty result is a valid empty vector. The fixture retains ABC and discards XYZ at a threshold greater than two, and the retained ABC remains valid after the input is dropped. This avoids shoehorning a different operation into an unsuitable abstraction.

Reconstruct a working checkpoint

From the course root, create a fresh final P12 study copy. The helper preserves originals, copies the exact lockfile, and refuses to overwrite an existing destination. Reuse your prior copy or choose another name when repeating the exercise.

python3 scripts/start-checkpoint.py p12 final --destination learner-work/dispatch-investigation
mise exec -- cargo test --locked --all-targets --manifest-path learner-work/dispatch-investigation/Cargo.toml
mise exec -- cargo run --locked --manifest-path learner-work/dispatch-investigation/Cargo.toml --example dispatch_allocation

The P12 checkpoint guide also provides the earlier exact-price milestone. Mise keeps build output in the shared native target.

When you get stuck

Run the example tests, then reduce a borrowing failure to one symbol and one owner. Write down which value owns each buffer and the last use of each reference. Read the standard Vec and String documentation for allocation behavior, and the Reference for trait objects. A useful review request includes the smallest failing lifetime example, the required retention duration, your proposed ownership boundary, and whether your concern is compile time, memory, or runtime. Avoid asking for a performance patch before identifying the cost.

Engineering decisions, evidence limits, and mastery

This small parser uses no external dependency, accepts bounded input, preserves typed failures, and explicitly transitions from borrowed to owned records. Separate static and dynamic functions make dispatch choices visible for teaching; a real API may choose only one. The two example tests passed and the executable output was recorded in the example log. All P12 targets passed strict Clippy. No allocator instrumentation or static-versus-dynamic timing was collected, and no dispatch speedup is claimed.

Mastery means defending an ownership choice from a duration requirement, narrowing a zero-copy statement to the operation actually verified, and explaining why a borrowed trait object need not allocate. You should also recognize when the metric abstraction fails to express a new operation and simplify or reshape it instead of adding a misleading implementation.
